question: Since the first recent outbreaks of lumpy skin disease (LSD) in France, livestock farmers have been required to carry out mass slaughter, including in cattle herds that were all correctly vaccinated in accordance with national and European health recommendations. In some cases, entire herds have been slaughtered due to one animal testing positive, despite strict adherence to vaccination rules.

This leads to significant economic loss, serious social difficulties and a feeling of injustice amongst the farmers concerned. In view of the above, can the Commission answer the following questions: 1.

Does it intend to formally refer the matter to the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) for an updated scientific opinion on: the effectiveness of the current LSD vaccines; the risk of transmission from vaccinated animals; the relevance, from a health perspective, of systematic slaughtering in correctly vaccinated herds; and the options for alternative, proportionate measures?
Does it have a consolidated economic assessment of the losses incurred from the LSDrelated mass slaughter in the EU since the recent outbreaks?
Is it considering a targeted financial support scheme for farmers affected by herd slaughtering despite correct vaccination?
Supporter1
This question is supported by a Member other than the authors: Julien Leonardelli (PfE).
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.4.2026)

The Commission refers the Honourable Members to the answers to Questions P-004688/20251, E-000029/20262 and P-004548/2025/rev.13, which outline the robust framework for lumpy skin disease (LSD) control established by EU legislation, aligned with World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) standards and supported by European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) assessments.

In addition, the Commission points out that EFSA4 has evaluated the effectiveness of control measures foreseen in that legal framework; it is on the basis of that scientific assessment that those measures are considered appropriate, notably effective and proportionate.

Experience of past and current outbreaks shows that the most effective way to prevent more serious and widespread economic losses, safeguard the internal market, and restore diseasefree status quickly is to implement the mandatory control and eradication measures immediately and to deploy vaccination quickly.
As also indicated in the reply to P-004688/2025, EU financial support is available under the Single Market Programme5 and the measures under the Common Agricultural Policy6.
